lines.text: Start with $\mathbf{w}$ as suits the problem, e.g. $\mathbf{0}$
take the action $\pi$ gives for $S$; see $R$ and $S'$

verification.note: Compared with the text layer of Figure 9.1; checks ch09.ex9-1, ch09.ex9-2 and ch09.ex9-4 confirm its tabular, aggregation and off-line special cases.

explainer.problem: Estimate $v_\pi$ when there are too many states for a table, by adjusting a small parameter vector from TD errors.

example.text: With one feature per state it is exactly tabular TD(λ): on the 19-state walk the weights equal the tabular values after every episode (Exercise 9.1).

advantages: Generalizes: one update changes the values of many states.
Linear and on-policy: converges, with error within (9.9) of the best.
limitations: For λ < 1 the target is biased, so it is not a true gradient method.
With other state distributions it can diverge (Chapter 10, unwritten in this draft).

comparisons.point: Tabular TD(λ) is the case of one-hot features.
The same update for action values, with action selection added.

name: Linear, gradient-descent Sarsa(λ) with binary features

lines.text: $\mathbf{w}$ and $\mathbf{e}$ have one component per feature; start with $\mathbf{w}$ e.g. $\mathbf{0}$
$\mathbf{e} \leftarrow \mathbf{0}$; choose $S$ and $A$ (e.g. ε-greedy); $F_A \leftarrow$ the features present in $S, A$
take $A$; see $R$ and $S'$; $\delta \leftarrow R - \sum_{i \in F_A} w_i$
for each action $a$ in $S'$: $F_a \leftarrow$ features present in $S', a$; $Q_a \leftarrow \sum_{i \in F_a} w_i$

verification.note: Compared with the text layer of Figure 9.8; Example 9.2 is reproduced by checks ch09.mountain-car and ch09.fig9-11.

explainer.problem: On-policy control in a continuous state space: learn approximate action values from binary features and act ε-greedily on them.

example.text: Mountain car with ten 9 × 9 tilings, replacing traces with clearing, λ = 0.9, ε = 0, α = 0.05: the first 10 episodes average over 400 steps, episodes 91–100 under 80.

advantages: Cheap: only the m present features enter each value.
Solves mountain car within about 100 episodes.
limitations: No convergence proof for this control method (bibliographical remarks).
Accumulating traces can blow up at larger α and λ (Figure 9.11).

comparisons.point: Tabular Sarsa(λ) is the case of one feature per state–action pair.
Watkins's Q(λ) uses the max and cuts traces after exploratory actions.

name: Linear, gradient-descent Watkins's Q(λ) with binary features

lines.text: $\mathbf{w}$ and $\mathbf{e}$ have one component per feature; start with $\mathbf{w}$ e.g. $\mathbf{0}$
for each action $a$: $F_a \leftarrow$ features present in $S, a$; $Q_a \leftarrow \sum_{i \in F_a} w_i$
$A^* \leftarrow \arg\max_a Q_a$; $A \leftarrow A^*$ with probability $1 - \varepsilon$, else a random action

verification.note: Compared with the text layer of Figure 9.9; check ch09.watkins-linear confirms it learns the mountain-car task.

explainer.problem: Off-policy control with linear function approximation: learn about the greedy policy while exploring.

example.text: On mountain car (ten 9 × 9 tilings, replacing traces, λ = 0.9, α = 0.05, ε = 0.05) episodes 91–100 average under 120 steps, from over 300 at first.

advantages: Learns about the greedy policy while behaving ε-greedily.
limitations: Q-learning with function approximation is known not to be sound and can diverge (bibliographical remarks).

comparisons.point: Sarsa(λ) never cuts traces and bootstraps from the action actually chosen.
